lesson.grammar_point: relative clauses for precise technical description

listenings.text: The best explanation of a payment system I ever heard was given by somebody with no slides at all, because the projector had failed. He said one sentence and then he stopped. The sentence was: money leaves the client, sits in three places on the way, and arrives two days later. That was it. And then he said, I will tell you about any of the three places you want, in any order. What that did was extraordinary. Everybody in the room understood the shape before they heard a single detail, so every detail after that had somewhere to go. Compare that with what usually happens, which is a diagram with forty boxes on it and a presenter who starts at the top left corner. Nobody follows that. Not because it is complicated, but because the shape arrives last.

Taking questions in a second language is the part people dread, and almost all of the fear comes from one thing, which is the belief that you have to answer immediately. You do not. There are three moves that buy you as much time as you need and none of them makes you look weaker. The first is to repeat the question back in your own words, which gives you five seconds and also checks that you understood it. The second is to say which part you will answer first, when the question has two halves. And the third, and this is the one nobody uses, is to say honestly that you do not have that number, name the person who does, and say when you will come back. A director who says I do not know, Marina owns that, I will send it on Thursday sounds more senior than one who improvises. Improvising is what junior people do.

I run architecture for a mid-sized bank, and I want to say something about the word workaround, because I hear it used as an apology and it should not be. Every institution older than fifteen years is full of workarounds, and each one exists because somebody solved a real problem quickly, with what they had. The mistake is not having them. The mistake is not knowing where they are. When a supplier asks me what our architecture looks like, I do not describe the ideal picture, I describe the real one, including the two places where a person still moves a file by hand every morning. It costs me nothing to say that, and it saves both of us three months. And I will tell you what actually happens when you do it: the good suppliers relax, because now they can plan, and the weak ones change the subject.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: a temporary solution somebody built because the proper one did not exist
a long document that explains how something works and why it was designed that way
the moment one team passes the work to another
the whole journey, from the first click to the money arriving
the one point that limits everything after it
the picture that shows which system talks to which
something that has to happen first, or nothing else can move
the specific place where the current process hurts the people using it

paras: There is a way of explaining a complicated system that works in any language, and a way that fails in all of them. The one that fails starts at the top left corner of an architecture diagram and works across. The one that works gives the shape first, in a single sentence, and only then opens it up.

Anneke Vos, who has run integration projects for four banks, puts it in one line: “Money leaves the client, sits in three places on the way, and arrives two days later.” That is the whole system. Everything after it is detail, and detail has somewhere to go now. She then invites the room to choose: “I can take you through any of the three places, in any order.” The room that has heard the shape can follow the end-to-end process; the room that has not is still trying to read the boxes.

The second half of the technique is being honest about the parts that are ugly. Every institution older than fifteen years is full of workarounds, and each one exists because somebody solved a real problem quickly with what they had. “The mistake is not having them,” Vos says. “The mistake is not knowing where they are.” She names the two places where a person still moves a file by hand every morning, because a supplier who knows that can plan around it, and one who does not will discover it in month four and bill for it.

The same honesty applies to the dependencies. If the reporting change has to land before the platform migration can start, that is not a detail to be mentioned in the appendix; it is the sentence that decides the whole timeline. And a bottleneck is worth naming out loud for the same reason: the one point which limits everything after it is the only place where money spent actually changes the result.

None of this requires a whitepaper. Vos says she has read hundreds and remembers three. What she remembers instead are the presentations where somebody said the shape in one sentence, named the pain point without decorating it, and then answered questions for forty minutes without a slide.
